 Blog Post · October 22, 2026
 Experts Shed Light on Recent Upticks in Late-Arriving Mail Ballots
 Mary Severance 
 Subscribe to our blog →
 View Larger
 Mary Severance 
 Mary Severance 
 Only a small number of vote-by-mail ballots in California are rejected because they are postmarked or returned too late—but recent increases have raised questions and concerns. Recently, PPIC’s Eric McGhee and the Center for Inclusive Democracy’s Mindy Romero discussed a new report that assesses possible causes and looks at which voters are most likely to have their ballots rejected for lateness.
 As McGhee noted, California’s long history of voting by mail began in 1978, when the state introduced “no excuse” absentee voting. In 2015, the state began allowing counties to count ballots postmarked on Election Day and arriving up to three days thereafter. This reduced the state’s late-ballot rejection rate from .45% to .21%.
 In several recent elections, however, rejection rates have increased—despite the seven-day post–Election Day arrival window that has been in place since 2022. This has raised concerns and questions about whether late ballots are coming from particular parts of the state and/or are associated with particular voter demographics.
 The report found that a geographic pattern emerged in the 2025 special election—the first election after the US Postal Service rolled out its Regional Transportation Optimization (RTO) plan in California; RTO has reduced mail collection in rural areas to once a day by eliminating end-of-day pick-ups. In these areas, a ballot mailed in the afternoon on Election Day might not be postmarked until the next day, and would therefore be rejected for lateness.
 The counties that had higher late-ballot rejection rates in 2025 do tend to be farther from regional processing centers and to have more zip codes that are affected by RTO.
 “There is a geographic pattern that emerged in the 2025 special election, in terms of late-ballot rejection, that was not present in 2022 or 2024,” said McGhee. “That increases our concern that RTO is playing a role.” However, only about a quarter of all mailed ballots came from RTO zip codes, so RTO explains only 19% of the total statewide increase from 2024 to 2025.
 Are any voter characteristics associated with late-ballot rejection rates? McGhee noted that all of the factors considered—age, experience with voting, party affiliation, race/ethnicity—are interrelated: “Younger voters are more likely to be no-party-preference, more likely to have less experience voting, and more likely to be voters of color.” But age turns out to be the most important single predictor of late-arriving ballots.
 “By definition, young voters are new to the voting process,” said report coauthor Mindy Romero. “We don’t do a good job in California in educating young voters through the schooling process.”
 What can California do to address the late-ballot trend? Romero and McGhee noted that state and local officials, advocates, and community groups can encourage voters to mail ballots early (at least a week ahead) or take them to drop boxes or staffed locations. “We should make a special effort to reach young people and people in RTO zip codes,” said McGhee.
 In the longer term, election officials should keep pushing for USPS evening pick-up in RTO zip codes on Election Day. “We also should do more research on mail delivery times, because something else may be increasing mail ballot rejection,” said McGhee. “It deserves a closer look.”
